💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement.
  • César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan claims when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine.
  • It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement.

César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan claims when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.

It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he indicates. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.

Recent findings suggest that “I get up, take them to school, go to the gym. I do pilates some days. I walk the dogs, play golf, then it’s after-school activities. I read, try to learn new things. I haven’t yet thought: ‘I’m bored,’” Azpilicueta states, although you wonder how long that will last. “Over the last 12 months I could see it. The summer before I already ‘hit the post’ with retirement. It’s natural: a day comes … if only I could play for ever but it is what it is and you have to keep evolving. I’m enjoying it.”.

Industry observers note that don’t get the wrong idea. “In terms of controlling your time, playing every three days, always waiting on the next message: ‘Meet at …,’ it’s a release. But it’s not a liberation because you’re delighted to pull your boots on. An vital part of your life ends; you kick a ball almost from the moment you walk, live your passion. Even last season – when there were days everything hurt, when you think: ‘How can I get injured like that?’.

– I would make demands of myself, my teammates. I always liked that.

“I never thought I’d be a professional. I couldn’t tell you the moment I thought: ‘I’m a footballer,’” Azpilicueta states, but he can tell you the score on his debut, for Osasuna in 2007. “One-nil win, Getafe.” Celta Vigo were the last opponents: a 1-0 loss in May for Sevilla. Between those, more than 800 matches, 508 for Chelsea. Only five players have played more for Chelsea; no foreigner has.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I,” Azpilicueta indicates, and there’s that laugh again. It’s a long time since he stood before his newly introduced teammates and sang an Estopa track. He arrived in London with a labrador and a sausage dog; he left a legend and the captain, with three kids and every trophy, a European and world champion.

Sources indicate that asked to define his career in a word, Azpilicueta goes for: constancia. Perseverance, consistency, commitment. He talks about the cruciate tear with Marseille aged 21 as a lesson, something that “changed my perspective and made me value discipline, preparation … Out of something negative I grew.” About always adapting, always overcoming, becoming what managers need you to be. There’s a laugh at the little lies – of course I’ve played on the left, boss – and the hours spent alone practising, convincing coaches or teammates to stay behind with him and go over it again and again.

It has been revealed that “I arrived at Chelsea late in the market [in 2012],” Azpilicueta says. “My representative stated: ‘We’ve spoken to Michael Emenalo, the sporting director, and they’re signing younger players.’ Oscar, Eden Hazard, Victor Moses, Marko Marin, Paulo Ferreira. I was 22. Doubts? Pfff … Olympique needed the money. Chelsea had just won the Champions League and I …”.

Sources indicate that that laugh. “I hadn’t played for Spain. What did Emenalo see in me? It’s hard to work it out. Also, what you are and what you become is different. You think: ‘What’s it going to be like?’ Another country, another pace, but Juan Mata was there, Fernando Torres, Oriol [Romeu]. Dr [Paco] Biosca, Ivan the physio. Petr Cech spoke Spanish. Hazard and I spoke French together. I could [communicate] with the Brazilians. But it wasn’t just them. I integrated fast, tried to speak English.

Recent findings suggest that “Not long after arriving there was this audience with fans. Fernando, Juan, Oriol and I. A Q&A. One said: ‘Look, your name is very difficult. Can we just call you Dave?’ Juan translated. I said: ‘Yeah, sure,’ thinking that they meant for the evening. And it stuck. Going down the street: ‘Hey, Dave!’ There was the occasional ‘Dave’ in the dressing room but mostly it was fans. I felt the affection.

Recent findings suggest that “You go with an open mind and bit by bit carve yourself a place. Every time a new coach comes you think: ‘Now what? Will I fit?’ I started as a winger in Pamplona. At Chelsea I played right-back, left-back, a line of three which I hadn’t played in my life … lots of systems, lots of coaches.”.

It has been revealed that twelve coaches, in fact. Azpilicueta played under all of them. “You arrive at a historic club like Chelsea and just try to stay as long as you can. That machine makes demands of you every three days. What I really noticed was a hunger to win: either you have that culture or … forget it. At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe. You see teammates come and go. The reality is the reality. On the pitch, you have to do it. It’s hard? Yes. But you can’t be sunk by a bad game. If you win: very good, done, next. If you can’t perform, you’re out … You have to manage that pressure.

Industry observers note that “I’ve had plenty of unpleasant days. I remember a 6-0 loss to Manchester City.” So then what? “For me, the first thing would be watch the video. Look at the data. But know that’s not everything. Sleep, get up, turn it round. Get into training first. And it’s not just about you; some days it’s about lifting up teammates too.”.

According to recent reports, preparation, he says, was fundamental. “I analysed everything. I want to know if when the winger receives, he turns left. I needed that. Football’s not mathematical – ‘this equals that’ – but that information helps you have more control, feel readier. I don’t know if I was more [serious] than others, but I was very cuadriculado, square. Others hardly did anything and were fine.”.

Recent findings suggest that that sounds like Hazard. Azpilicueta laughs. “He was more … more … relaxed. Not everyone has to be the same. I was very square, I prepared differently, I was like a robot.”.

Besides, Hazard was the best; it is his name, not Lionel Messi or Ronaldo’s, that comes up when Azpilicueta is asked his toughest opponent. “I was fortunate to train with Eden. He didn’t train 100%, but he forced you to. I had to kick him sometimes, haha! Playing together, he would say: ‘Give me the ball.’ I would say: ‘Stay there, I’ll defend for you.’”.

Azpilicueta defended them all. “The first time I was captain was an FA Cup semi-final against Tottenham [in 2017],” he claims. “We arrived late, no one mentioned anything. [Gary] Cahill, the captain, was injured. We walk in and, pam, the armband’s in my place. Steve Holland says: ‘Let’s go to the referees meeting.’ ‘Oh, OK’ … and that was it. I liked it. I don’t think you change much; you have your own personality. You don’t have to score two because you’re captain. Besides, that was a one-off until later. But you do feel a little extra responsibility.”.

Fresh players found Azpilicueta waiting for them, leadership through empathy and example. “Quite a few stayed at my house,” he notes. But if there is a portrait of his leadership perhaps it is him paying for the bus, covering petrol for the first team and youth team, when Chelsea’s assets were frozen after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And his reaction to that being put to him now. “Nah,” he says. “Well. No. All of us. I didn’t do anything anyone else didn’t. We did it together, which is how things should be done.

“There a feeling of: ‘We have this matter, we’re going to sort this out,’” Azpilicueta notes, fist hitting the desk. “That situation was strange. We had won the Club World Cup, been with [Roman Abramovich] there and suddenly … it was the uncertainty: players, staff. Many people work for Chelsea, depend on that.”.

Underlying it all is the same basic principle, Azpilicueta says: “People. There are so many day-to-day who make it work. And sure, we’re good at football but what really fulfils you is see people there with their families all together when you win, when you lift the Champions League.”.

Have you got a photo of you lifting that cup? “At home? No. A friend gave me a very nice one framed but it’s half hidden. I don’t much like showing it off.” If someone came to your house could they tell a footballer lives there? “No.”.

According to recent reports, twenty years on, a lifetime later, a footballer doesn’t. So now what? “I don’t know,” Azpilicueta states, laughing. “Maybe I’ll be here, playing off a better handicap. But I like football, being involved. I’ve done some co-commentating. I have the MBA, the diploma. Not because I necessarily want to be a sporting director tomorrow, but because it interests me, because it’s nice to learn. I enjoyed the classes, meeting people, doing course work.”.

In a recent development, the practical experience is even better. “The last few contracts I negotiated myself. I’ve had various agents help over the years but a time came with Chelsea when I thought: ‘What for?’ I sit down with Marina [Granovskaia], then with Behdad [Eghbali] and Todd [Boehly]. As captain I had spoken to them about so many problems that when it came to my own I thought: ‘I can do this alone.’ I might have got a better deal, who knows, but I was comfortable that way. I was never looking for anything, I was happy, my family was happy, I felt loved and valued and that was it. I just wanted to go in to work every day.”.

On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA releases MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18, 2013, NASA debuted the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.
  • In a recent development, the name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN.
  • MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Nov. 18, 2013, NASA debuted the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

In a recent development, the name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

In a recent development, solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

It has been revealed that after its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

Sources indicate that "The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, stated in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come.".

Industry observers note that MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

An investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

"Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, remarked of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here.".

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. She presently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

It has been revealed that “All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese stated. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

Industry observers note that “So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”.

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship.

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

According to recent reports, in the same game, Clark stated to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

Sources indicate that “Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese noted. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”.

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark mentioned in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it highlights. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

According to recent reports, “But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”.

LSU head coach Mulkey mentioned she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”.

Reese mentioned the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit.
  • Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.
  • This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the upcoming head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit.

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the upcoming head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.

Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick.

Industry observers note that eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.

It has been revealed that very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.

The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.

Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.

Yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.

“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.

Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.

By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s fresh project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.

After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.

Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.

In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.

Going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.

It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.

Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.

They were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.

It has been revealed that A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.

This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.

Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.

De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a upcoming study reports.
  • As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Latest York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a upcoming study reports.

As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Latest York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

Recent findings suggest that in the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

Sources indicate that in 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

According to recent reports, the researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

In a recent development, then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar stated.

In a recent development, in the new study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

Industry observers note that now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar said. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

According to recent reports, the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four, but at least against Fulham they ended a three-game losing run. As they await their fate after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped. This passive draw was met with boos from the home fans.

Sources indicate that arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence. They had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.

It is the first time Fulham have avoided defeat against City in 21 attempts going back to 2011, while City have conceded in nine consecutive games for the first time since 2019. Enzo Maresca and his side’s problems go beyond legal wrangling.

City approached the game in the same subdued manner of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. They offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of half chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game as slow-starters City conceded the opener for a fourth straight match.

It has been revealed that confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems under Maresca, who saw Marc Guéhi cross the halfway line to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first header, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on.

In the 16th ​minute, Oscar Bobb, a former City winger, shimmied and Muniz curled his shot into the top corner from the edge of the box.

Recent findings suggest that city finally found intent midway through the first half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp. Thomas Bramall and the video assistant referee gave the keeper the benefit of the doubt. Leno later told BBC Sport: “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me. It was a wet pitch. I was hoping VAR doesn’t overturn it. For me it was a foul.”.

• Fulham avoided defeat against Manchester City for the first time since September 2011 in all competitions, ending the longest ever winning streak one team has had against another in English football (20 matches).

• Manchester City have conceded in nine consecutive games in all competitions for the first time since a run to December 2019 (10), while they have conceded the opening goal in four consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run to April 2012 (5).

Recent findings suggest that • Manchester City have trailed at half-time in four consecutive Premier League games for only the third time, after October 1995 and April 2006. Opta.

Maresca disagreed. “From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not foul but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately,” he said.

City lacked a cutting edge. Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, could not get on the same wavelength as the misfiring Haaland, whose clinical finishing deserted him.

City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, snuffing out every danger. To find a way back, City needed to increase the tempo and Anderson obliged by volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.

In an underperforming team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst. He latched on to a Haaland flick-on but could not stay on his feet. The pair combined for a second time only for Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish to end with the ball slipping an inch wide in the 65th minute, City’s last meaningful opportunity.

As the game ebbed to a close, City’s flaws were exposed as Fulham won the ball and Muniz was through on goal. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after as Fulham continued to look sharp and City blunt.

The jeers at the end remarked it all.

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty.
  • Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.
  • Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty.

Net zero is no longer enough. Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.

Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years. Reaching net-zero status would halt the rise in temperatures. But only achieving net-negative status can bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C threshold this century.

Recent findings suggest that can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

Can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

It has been revealed that that reality has made net negative and the enormous amount of CO2 removal that would be needed to achieve it a prominent idea at the summit. A coalition of eight countries called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE) has been working to convince other nations to adopt net-negative targets and get serious about CO2 removal. The group unveiled that it will be co-chaired by Denmark and Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s climate summit and could put net negative at the top of the agenda.

“We are in an era of overshoot, and we have to do a lot in terms of removing carbon dioxide,” Ethiopian ambassador Samuel Addis Alemayehu said at a GONE event on 18 November, touting the nation’s progress on reforestation.

Some climate campaigners worry that CO2 removal technologies won’t work and that focusing on them could distract countries from cutting emissions. Despite those concerns, the latest draft of the main statement from COP31 recognizes that CO2 removal has a role in addressing the overshoot, and welcomes efforts to “urgently and rapidly” scale up development of removal methods.

According to a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report1 released ahead of the meeting, the world can expect about 1.8 °C of warming this century, even in the most optimistic emissions scenario.

Recent findings suggest that every fraction of a degree above 1.5 °C raises the risk of climate disasters such as wildfires and powerful hurricanes. “COP31 will be judged a failure if we don’t address the overshoot,” stated Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the UN and chair of the Association of Small Island States, at a press briefing held during the summit.

It has been revealed that many countries at the meeting have discussed slashing emissions to limit the size and duration of the coming overshoot. Turkey has pushed to implement a target of 35% of global energy demand being met with electricity by 2035, a proposal that has gained support from more than 75 countries at the conference and is also included in the draft statement.

But the UNEP report estimates that to recover from overshoot, at least 330 billion tonnes of CO2 would have to be pulled out of the atmosphere this century after the world reaches net zero. Removing that much CO2 would require a vast expansion of existing efforts. Today, about two billion tonnes of CO2 per year are removed by nature-based projects such as reforestation, which takes advantage of the carbon absorbed by growing trees. Scaling up carbon removal promptly enough to achieve net negative and storing carbon in a more durable form will require technological CO2 removal solutions as well.

Tech Report: Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs.
  • "We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.
  • Weinswig mentioned retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of major-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig mentioned retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of major-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

According to recent reports, "It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig mentioned. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year.".

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Recent findings suggest that most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit fresh record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology tech giant OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania mentioned.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives noted.

Industry observers note that UPS CEO Carol Tomé said on the firm's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers.".

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for massive-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company's annual forecast. Leathers noted even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

It has been revealed that "The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers remarked. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf.".

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

Recent findings suggest that it's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding fresh team members.

Industry observers note that "Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania mentioned.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry.".

Amit Regev, CEO of drone tech giant Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev said. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones.".

'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin: Europe remains committed to Ukraine

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19).
  • Extensive security measures have already been revealed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants.
  • Recent findings suggest that the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.

Extensive security measures have already been revealed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.

Recent findings suggest that the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London.

It has been revealed that but what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic.

"The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no plan outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises.".

Nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.

Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.

This has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)?

Recent findings suggest that after the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz stated: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear.".

Recent findings suggest that but what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part.

Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate notes a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under.

"Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister remarked. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that.".

German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator.

At the federal government's regular press briefing, he stated: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week.

Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he said: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.".

Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question.".

Recent findings suggest that hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.

According to recent reports, european supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the glitch is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.

According to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the issue, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.

Sources indicate that A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing matter in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.

Tech Report: Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world.
  • Sources indicate that social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs.
  • In an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world. With movies like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, The Land Before Time, All Dogs Go to Heaven, and Anastasia, this American animator offered us realms of adventure, with plucky heroes as well as villains so fantastically frightening that we carry the thrill of it all with us decades later.

Sources indicate that social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs. Brisby being chased down by monstrous, roaring, ravenous cats. Now, for fans upcoming and old, filmmakers Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker offer Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, a documentary that explores the life and work of the innovative animator through his own words.

In an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues. Together, they pursued animation not for the money but for the art and a deep desire to create something meaningful for future generations. Yet, when asked about his legacy, Bluth is quick to look back on the path that led him to his work.

Sources indicate that he began by speaking of Winsor McCay, the father of American animation. In a wistful storyteller tone, Bluth recounted how a little boy witnessed the "magic" of the 1914 short film Gertie the Dinosaur, in which a pencil-sketched brontosaurus comes to life. This little boy was so inspired that he'd grow up to make his own animated short featuring a mouse named Mickey.

Industry observers note that that little boy, of course, was Walt Disney, who would go on to make 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first animated feature film produced in the United States. That movie would go on to inspire a young Bluth, who'd direct his first animated feature in 1982 with The Secret of NIMH.

This path of inspiration to iconic art wasn't as direct a line as you might think.

Yes, Bluth scored a dream job, working at Disney Animation studio for 10 years on films like Sleeping Beauty, Robin Hood, and The Rescuers. But after Disney's death in 1966, Bluth and 17 other Disney animators feared the studio had lost their way, creatively.

It has been revealed that he told Mashable he'd invite these artists to his home on weekends, where they'd draw together to develop innovative pitches for their corporate bosses. When they were shot down, Bluth — along with Gary Goldman and John Pomeroy — built their own tech giant, Don Bluth Productions, to "see if we could do better than they were doing." For this, Bluth remembered, "We were called traitors.".

It has been revealed that that's not how Bluth saw his team. "[These] wonderful people had the courage to leave their jobs and security and go out there and try and do something great," he remarked, "not just to feed their egos, but something they felt helped them grow up. And they wanted to give back.".

It has been revealed that it was not an easy journey, as Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There details, revealing the highs and lows of Bluth's most beloved and worst-reviewed productions, as well as the wildly popular video game Dragon's Lair. In our interview, he spoke repeatedly about how the doc filled him with gratitude as he looked back for the filmmakers' interviews.

To Mashable, he reflected, "What happened after so many movies, All Dogs Go to Heaven, American Tail, working with Steven Spielberg on both of those pictures, and George Lucas [on The Land Before Time], [it] became really, really obvious to us that we were doing the right thing [by] writing the right stories, and trying to make something that would move people's lives for the better — not just to pat our own backs and say, 'Look what we did.' [We were making] something that would help maybe children grow up and have some degree of morality about them. So then, that was our goal in everything.".

It has been revealed that in Somewhere Out There, the rise of computer animation — which Bluth refers to as "3D animation" — came as a devastating blow to the animator, who'd spent his life developing the skills of hand-drawn 2D animation. To this day, Bluth still advocates for the artistry of hand-drawn animation.

"The way I look at this is animation in the 2D form is people, armed with a pencil in their hands, have to be able to draw," he explained, "and they also have to be able to act. And they have to have feelings about story.".

To Bluth, CGI movies aren't animation. "3D animation is puppetry," he said, adding, "[With 3D animation,] you drop your pencil. You put your hands on a keyboard, and you make a wireframe puppet act.".

In a recent development, bluth shared several of his complaints about the look of 3D animation, saying, "To me, it looks very plastic... The colors are muted, and they're trying to put shading in there, trying to look more like a live-action picture." He asked, "Why are we trying to get to a place which looks more real?" adding, "That isn't the purpose at all of 2D [animation]. The purpose is to take you to a magical world. 2D is trying to make audiences come to our own world.".

In a recent development, noting the animation industry changed forever with the massive success of 1995's Toy Story, Bluth said, "Toy Story [movies] were quite fun to watch, but they didn't make me feel anything very deep. And animation is intended to do that, particularly with Walt Disney pictures. Snow White, Bambi, [and] Pinocchio — those pictures did something to change the way you thought and help you grow up in a way that was really good. And they did it in such a beautiful way.".

Sources indicate that it was when Disney Studios, post-Walt, moved away from these tenets that Bluth and his colleagues set out on their own. He said, "We left the Disney Studio because it was leaving out the morality statements and leaving out all the beautiful colors and everything.".

In terms of what recent animated films impressed Bluth, he mentioned, "I liked Klaus a lot," commending Sergio Pablos' inventive Christmas tale, which employs hand-drawn animation with a unique visual style.

According to recent reports, bluth also enjoyed Pete Docter's 2009 Pixar hit Up. "That was totally in 3D," he noted, "but it had a great story. For my taste, it went on too long. You know, the story was really about this couple promising each other they would go back to some place in their life, and she died. So, the man, true to the promise, tries to fulfill that [by taking their house on the journey]. So, I love that.".

Sources indicate that overall though, Bluth lamented, "Animation has become an advertisement for sugar cereal and whatever. There are more advertisements on animation than there are actually animated characters. The animated characters are just simply little puppets that jump up and down and tell one-line jokes. So, that's not good. Now, the last laugh is about to hit us like a tsunami; that is AI.".

Through the stories of Russian Jewish immigrant Fievel Mousekewitz, the widowed mother of four Mrs. Brisby, the orphaned brontosaurus Littlefoot, and rogue mutt Charlie B. Barkin, Bluth was striving to create stories that would inspire children to be good and creative, as Disney's movies had done for him. He doesn't see a future where AI can provide such mindful, moral guidance.

"It seems like AI is able to do wonderful, wonderful things," Bluth mused, "except AI is a machine, and it has no soul. It will borrow or steal, if you will, from everything that it knows, and give you what you ask for. But where's the creativity?".

Industry observers note that "AI is a borrower," Bluth explained. "When you enter what you'd like to see, it searches all over and borrows it from other artists, puts it together. It shows you on screen. Now, you can then make corrections. It can do all that, but it is still a machine. It doesn't ask you, 'Well, what is right and wrong? What is evil and good? What do you want me to say?' The machine can't do that.".

It has been revealed that he continued, "The only thing you can do is go back to human beings and say, 'Don't replace human beings with machines.' They're the ones who have a heart, who have a soul, and probably have a Creator. So, there's a bigger picture that's going on than just animation on a screen.".

"AI has no soul," Bluth concluded. "It hasn't a clue how to write anything. Everything that you're going to see on your screen has been stolen from other artists.".

He allowed that some AI might be "stunningly beautiful," but "you'll find that it doesn't affect your heart the way you feel… They're not artists that are doing the AI. Many of them don't understand the art of acting or anything. So, what everything looks like in AI animation that I've seen, it all looks like slow motion, and it looks unreal. So, that's definitely a road I don't want to travel on.".

"I read somewhere where someone said something that stuck in my head," he mused, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde's The Portrait of Dorian Gray. "There are many people who know the price of everything but the value of nothing. And I certainly hope that's not where we're going.".

Marco Rose saluted the in-form Evanilson after the Brazilian scored for a sixth Premier League game in a row to lift Bournemouth up to fourth place with a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.

Evanilson’s brilliantly taken 19th-minute opener set his side on course for a club record ninth straight win in all competitions, while the defeat means Forest are only above the relegation places on goal difference having failed to build on the momentum of their 3-1 win against Manchester City before the international break.

It has been revealed that rose said: “We defend together as a team, and we attack together as a team, but the forward guys were excellent today. They did a great job scoring the goals and the other guys support them. Evanilson creates space, carries the ball, provides assists and now he scores goals as a No 9, really beautiful goals so I am happy.”.

Both teams started the game on the front foot and Forest had the first sight of goal. Neco Williams nodded dangerously across the face of goal at the far post, but Liam Delap was beaten to the ball by home defender Antonio Silva.

Evanilson was denied by a brilliant last-ditch tackle from Forest centre-back Jair Cunha before Marcus Tavernier’s 20-yard curler was well saved by Matz Sels.

Bournemouth took the lead in the 19th minute. James Hill cushioned a header into the path of Evanilson, and the Brazilian took one touch before blasting a left-foot shot into the roof of the net.

Industry observers note that justin Kluivert almost doubled the home side’s lead with an effort from 20 yards which sailed narrowly over the crossbar. Evanilson then failed to keep his shot down after a long throw from Hill caused chaos in the Forest penalty area.

Oliver Glasner’s side had a penalty appeal waved away when Adam Smith blocked Williams’s effort into the arm of teammate Tyler Adams. But Kluivert did make it 2-0 on the stroke of half-time with a simple far-post finish after a superb run and cross from Tavernier.

Recent findings suggest that forest were much improved in the second half, adopting a more direct approach in a bid to find a way back into the game. Delap turned provider by whipping in a cross for Morgan Gibbs-White but the captain could not properly connect with his header.

Sources indicate that • Bournemouth have won five successive games in the top-flight of English football for the first time. Only Arsenal (67, before Newcastle game) and Manchester City (60) have collected more Premier League points in 2026 than the Cherries (52 – W13 D13 L4).

• Bournemouth have won each of their last nine games in all competitions, their longest ever such run, overtaking two separate runs of eight in 1998-99 and 2012-13.

Industry observers note that • Nottingham Forest failed to score in this game despite registering 2.14 expected goals, the highest xG tally by any team not to score in a Premier League match this season. Opta.

James McAtee ballooned an effort over the bar as the visitors continued to misfire in front of goal. The substitute Chris Wood also miscued a header from a corner when he should have at least tested the underworked Bournemouth goalkeeper, Djordje Petrovic.

Sources indicate that bournemouth always looked a threat on the counter and Kluivert came close to his second and Bournemouth’s third when he stung the gloves of Sels from 18 yards out. Kluivert should also have been more clinical when he found himself within finishing range but unselfishly laid the ball off to Rayan and the chance went begging.

Glasner, whose side had 19 shots but only one on target, said: “Of course when you lose it’s always a tough 90 minutes, especially when you make too many mistakes like we did in the first half.

“The second goal straight before half-time was a little bit of a killer but credit to the lads in the second half for finding a filter back into the game. We had some good situations, but we couldn’t convert them.

According to recent reports, “We are not able to score in this game, and this is what we have to look at and where we have to improve. We took too many touches, and were not so aggressive.”.

Industry News: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.

Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space?

Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018.

"Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is crucial is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email.

Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email.

Recent findings suggest that "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.".

Industry observers note that the team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is.

In a recent development, each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Massive Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science.

Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1).

A JPL representative added that the "Significant Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space.

"Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did quickly recover.

Sources indicate that "The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause.".

Voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

According to recent reports, "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin noted in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather crucial details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of concerns.

Sources indicate that "One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he mentioned the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it.".

In a recent development, while there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team says it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd stated.

Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again.".

According to recent reports, editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.
